response.text:
Ishmael, a melancholy schoolmaster with a periodic urge to flee land’s confinements, chooses to sail. In New Bedford the Spouter-Inn’s smudged chaos and Father Mapple’s thunderous Jonah sermon announce strange waters. He shares a bed and then a bond with Queequeg, a tattooed harpooneer whose calm dignity and pagan rites enlarge his world. They sign aboard the bone-decorated Pequod, bargained on by canting Quakers Peleg and Bildad amid whispers of its unseen captain, Ahab. After chowder at the Try Pots and Queequeg’s Ramadan, the ship embarks on Christmas with a polyglot “democracy of hands” under three mates—careful Starbuck, jocular Stubb, and pugnacious Flask. That democracy will soon learn the cost of following one man’s will.

Ahab finally appears, scar-seamed and pegged to the deck by an ivory leg, his gaze boring through crew and horizon alike. He nails a Spanish ounce of gold to the mast and swears the men to hunt Moby Dick, while Starbuck feels blasphemy masquerading as purpose. Fedallah, a glistening-turbaned Parsee, rises with a hidden boat-crew and makes the captain’s private vow feel fated. The first lowering ends with a moonlit, teasing spout and a near-drowning, and from then on rumors and gams braid the Pequod to the White Whale’s wake. Ishmael catalogs heads and cases, mastheads and try-works, yet his learned digressions keep confessing the whale’s unpaintable mystery. Weaving a sword-mat with Queequeg and dreaming high in the rigging, he muses on fate and free will, until his famous meditation on the whiteness of the whale makes purity itself terrifying. The ship’s cosmopolitan fellowship mirrors the world it circles, even as Ahab’s monomania bends it toward one point and the sea’s beauty keeps revealing a universal cannibalism. When a vast, glimmering squid heaves up and sinks without a ripple, the air feels stained by omen, and the Pequod bears on toward Java and beyond.

Workaday whaling becomes a theater of omens: Stubb runs a sperm whale to a bloody flurry, the magical line smoking round a loggerhead, and the carcass is cut in by song and steel until a black Sphinx-head hangs alongside. Sharks frenzy at the try-works while old Fleece preaches to them and Stubb dines on steak, and Ahab leans over the severed brow to demand oracles from mute bone. The Pequod gams with the Jeroboam, whose Gabriel says the White Whale is a god, and with the Jungfrau, all brass and emptiness, then sails on into the Bashee Isles and Japan grounds. Pip, abandoned in a moment of fear and then plucked from the abyss, loses his wits and becomes the ship’s cracked conscience. Night at the try-works turns the vessel into a fire-ship and Ahab into a man who renounces instruments and charts, resolving that dead-reckoning and will shall steer him. A typhoon blackens the world, St. Elmo’s fire crowns the masts, and Ahab baptizes his harpoon in pagan blood and curses it in the devil’s name while Starbuck pleads prudence. In the calmer clangor that follows, the carpenter and blacksmith fashion a spare ivory leg and a new infernal iron, Pip nestles in the captain’s chair, and Queequeg’s coffin is carved, hooped, pitched, and finally rigged as the ship’s life-buoy. When lightning spoils the binnacle needles Ahab forges a new compass on deck, then turns away from the Rachel, whose Nantucket captain begs him to help find a twelve-year-old son. From that refusal the Pequod moves as if under a spell, the mates and pagan harpooneers extensions of Ahab’s will, while Fedallah’s murmur of two hearses and hemp worms into the captain’s mind. They raise the White Whale at last: the first day’s lowering tangles lines and snaps lives; the second day Moby Dick breaches like a snowy mountain, smashes boats, and Fedallah is found lashed dead to his back. At dawn of the third day Starbuck nearly mutinies and begs for home, but Ahab nails a fresh flag to the main-truck, musters new oars, and drives on.

In a roar of foam and circling sharks the White Whale dashes his forehead into the Pequod’s bow and then under her, holing the ship as the masthead harpooneers keep their posts to the last. Ahab casts his final iron; the line snarls round his neck; and he is jerked voiceless into the sea, from hell’s heart still stabbing in his thoughts. Tashtego, nailing the red flag to the sinking spar, snags a sky-hawk in the cloth and vanishes with mast and bird into the green vault as the sea rolls back. Cast off by the wreck, Ishmael finds Queequeg’s coffin-buoy bursting from the vortex and clings to it through a day and night until the Rachel, still searching for her lost boy, recovers another orphan. In the wake of that rescue the book binds its whaling ledger to its gospel: rites of flensing and forging become sacraments of defiance, the Pequod a chapel and charnel carried down by one will. Starbuck’s caution, Stubb’s gallows humor, Flask’s appetite, the pagan courage of Queequeg, Daggoo, and Tashtego, the Parsee’s fatal quiet, and Pip’s broken visions are gathered under one nailed doubloon and lost to one nailed fate, while the sea outlasts them, a void that draws the living on and leaves Ishmael to measure in cool prose how small a plank can bear a man back into human sight.
